summaryEn: Once one of Apple's principal metal casing suppliers, it now earns most of its reported profit from interest and investments rather than from manufacturing — operating margin 6.5%, net margin 40.7%. Revenue is down 55% year-on-year, and the shares trade at 0.73 times book.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + company disclosure; framing the post-casing transition honestly — the 40.69% net margin against a 6.45% operating margin identified as non-operating income, corroborated by the company's own explanation of FY2025's fall (FX turning negative, lower interest income, core operating profit stable), with collapsing revenue, negative operating cash flow and the 0.73× book valuation stated plainly; ★ a proven data defect — the feed's 2024Q4 EPS row carried the FY2024 ANNUAL figure of 19.40 — was stripped and the verified annual figures (FY2024 NT$19.40, FY2025 NT$11.33) used instead; sector Electronics Manufacturing → Metal Casings & Diversification)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Catcher Technology (可成科技, TWSE: 2474) built its business machining aluminium and magnesium into the casings of consumer electronics, and became one of the principal metal casing suppliers to the world's largest consumer electronics companies. Founded in **1984** and **listed in September 2001**, it is today something quite different, and the accounts say so plainly.

**In 2026Q1, Catcher reported an operating margin of 6.45% and a net margin of 40.69%.** That gap of more than thirty points is not an anomaly — it is the pattern. **2024Q4 showed 18.5% operating against 81.1% net; 2025Q1, 19.9% against 69.1%; 2025Q3, 15.2% against 61.1%; 2025Q4, 13.7% against 54.2%.** The company's reported profit comes overwhelmingly from **outside its operations** — interest income and investment returns on a very large financial asset base, together with foreign-exchange movements.

The company's own account confirms it. Explaining why **FY2025 EPS fell to NT$11.33 from FY2024's NT$19.40**, management attributed the decline to **foreign exchange swinging from positive to negative and reduced interest income**, noting that **core operating profit remained stable**. When a 42% fall in earnings is explained by interest and currency, the interest and currency are the earnings.

Meanwhile the operating business is shrinking fast. **Monthly revenue has fallen 21%, 25%, 36%, 48% and 55% year-on-year** over recent months; **May 2026 revenue was NT$918m, down 48.3%**, with **January–May cumulative revenue down 26.0% to NT$5.65bn**. 2025Q4 revenue of **NT$4.363bn** fell 10.2% sequentially on component shortages and customer year-end stocktaking. **2026Q1 operating cash flow was −NT$262m** despite **NT$1.54bn of reported net profit**.

Management is rebuilding around new markets — **medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and drones, and AI servers** — with new customer projects entering mass production from June and a **double-digit revenue contribution** expected for the year. A **share buyback is under way**.

The market's assessment is visible in the price. At **NT$184.50 the shares trade at 0.73× book** — **below the accounting value of the company's own assets** — on **NT$225.5bn of assets against NT$142.6bn of equity**, a **36.8% debt ratio**, and a **5.57% dividend yield** from a payout of **NT$10.27**. **Trailing return on equity is 4.11%.**

*(One data note: the metrics feed's 2024Q4 earnings-per-share entry carried NT$19.40, which is the **full-year FY2024 figure**, not the quarter. That row has been removed from this page; the verified annual figures are FY2024 **NT$19.40** and FY2025 **NT$11.33**.)*

The honest read: **a manufacturer that has largely finished being one, holding a large financial asset base that produces most of its profit — priced below book while it tries to build a new operating business.**

Catcher was founded in **1984** in Tainan, and made its name doing something difficult at enormous scale: **machining metal casings for consumer electronics**. A laptop or tablet casing milled from a solid aluminium billet requires vast numbers of CNC machines, tight tolerance control, consistent surface finish and the ability to ramp to millions of units for a product launch and then stop. Very few companies anywhere could do it, and the ones that could — Catcher among them — became essential suppliers to the world's largest consumer electronics brands. It **listed in 2001**.

The economics were extraordinary while they lasted, and they carried a structural weakness that every supplier in that position shares: **enormous fixed capital, one dominant customer relationship, and a product specification that the customer can change**. Metal casings gave way to different materials and constructions; assembly consolidated; and Chinese suppliers built comparable capability with domestic advantages. Catcher's casing business contracted.

What the company did with the proceeds is the reason it looks the way it does now. Rather than reinvesting in a declining business, it accumulated a **very large financial asset base** — the source of the **interest income** that management cites when explaining its earnings. **NT$225.5bn of assets** now sit against **NT$142.6bn of equity**, and the reported profit is dominated by what those assets earn rather than by what the factories produce.

That is why the income statement reads as it does: **a 6.45% operating margin and a 40.69% net margin in 2026Q1**, and a similar gap in every recent quarter. It is why management's explanation of FY2025's fall from **NT$19.40 to NT$11.33 per share** cited **foreign exchange and interest income** while describing **core operating profit as stable**.

The current effort is to build a new operating business around **medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and drones, and AI servers** — using the same precision metalworking competence for products with longer lifecycles and less customer concentration than consumer casings ever had.

- **1984 (23 Nov)** — Catcher Technology founded in Tainan, machining metal components and casings.
- **2001 (17 Sept)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2474)**.
- **2000s–2010s** — Becomes one of the principal metal casing suppliers to the world's largest consumer electronics companies, operating CNC machining at enormous scale. Dividends run **NT$10–12** annually through 2016–2020.
- **2020s** — The casing business contracts as materials, construction and supply arrangements change; the company accumulates a large financial asset base rather than reinvesting in a declining product.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$15.19**; dividend **NT$10.0**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$13.45**, including a **loss in Q4**; dividend **NT$10.0**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$19.40** (company-reported). Q4 shows an **81.1% net margin against an 18.5% operating margin**. Dividend raised to **NT$15.83**.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$11.33**, a 42% fall the company attributes to **foreign exchange turning negative and lower interest income**, with **core operating profit stable**. Q2 records a **loss of NT$1.60 per share**; Q4 revenue of **NT$4.363bn** falls 10.2% sequentially on component shortages and customer stocktaking. Dividend **NT$10.27**.
- **2026 (to June)** — Revenue collapse deepens: monthly declines of **21%, 25%, 36%, 48% and 55%**; **May revenue NT$918m (−48.3%)**; **January–May cumulative NT$5.65bn (−26.0%)**. **2026Q1 operating margin 6.45%, net margin 40.69%**, operating cash flow **−NT$262m**.
- **2026 (from June)** — New customer projects in **medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace/drones and AI servers** begin entering mass production, with a **double-digit revenue contribution** expected for the year. A **share buyback is under way**. Shares trade at **0.73× book**.

Catcher's accounts require the reader to separate **what the company earns** from **what the company does**.

- **The structural fact, stated first.** **2026Q1: operating margin 6.45%, net margin 40.69%.** The same gap appears in every recent quarter — **2024Q4 (18.5% vs 81.1%), 2025Q1 (19.9% vs 69.1%), 2025Q3 (15.2% vs 61.1%), 2025Q4 (13.7% vs 54.2%)**. Reported profit is dominated by **non-operating income**: interest and investment returns on a large financial asset base, plus foreign exchange.
- **The company's own explanation confirms it.** Management attributed **FY2025's fall from NT$19.40 to NT$11.33 per share** to **foreign exchange swinging from positive to negative and reduced interest income**, while stating that **core operating profit remained stable**. A 42% earnings decline explained by currency and interest is a decisive statement about where the earnings come from.
- **A data defect, found and corrected.** The metrics feed's **2024Q4 earnings-per-share entry read NT$19.40 — the FY2024 annual figure**, not the quarter. The proof is threefold: the company reported **FY2024 EPS of NT$19.40** and **FY2025 of NT$11.33**; the feed's four **2025** quarters sum to **11.36**, matching; and its four **2024** quarters sum to **33.28**, which does not. **That row has been removed**, and the verified annual figures are used throughout this page.
- **The operating business is contracting sharply.** Monthly revenue declines of **21%, 25%, 36%, 48% and 55%**; **May 2026 revenue NT$918m (−48.3%)**; **January–May cumulative NT$5.65bn (−26.0%)**. Gross margin remains respectable at **28.8%**, but on a rapidly shrinking base.
- **Cash flow does not follow the reported profit.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow was −NT$262m against NT$1.54bn of net income** — consistent with profit that originates outside operations.
- **A very large, lightly geared balance sheet.** **NT$225.5bn of assets** on **NT$142.6bn of equity**, a **36.8% debt ratio**, and **NT$16.18bn of cash** — with the remainder of the asset base in the financial and other holdings that generate the interest income.
- **A substantial dividend and a buyback.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$10.0 (2016) → 12.0 → 12.0 → 10.0 → 12.0 (2020) → 10.21 → 10.0 → 10.0 (2023) → 15.83 (2024) → NT$10.27 (2025)** — a **5.57% yield**. A **share buyback is under way**.
- **Priced below book.** **0.73× book** and **17.7× earnings**, with **trailing return on equity of 4.11%**.

The financing reality: **a large pool of assets earning a modest return, attached to a shrinking manufacturing business and a new one being built — valued by the market at less than the assets' stated worth.**

**Stance: a former consumer-electronics casing maker whose profit now comes mostly from interest and investments, with revenue down 55% year-on-year — trading at 0.73x book with a 5.57% yield while it builds a new operating business.**

The bull case:

1. **Priced below its own assets.** **0.73× book**, on **NT$142.6bn of equity** and **NT$225.5bn of assets** with a conservative **36.8% debt ratio**. The market values the company at less than the accounting worth of what it holds.
2. **The financial base produces real income.** Interest and investment returns are why the **net margin is 40.69% against a 6.45% operating margin** — and while that is not manufacturing profit, it is genuine income, and it funds a **5.57% dividend yield** and a **share buyback**.
3. **A credible diversification list.** **Medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and drones, AI servers** — all use precision metalworking, all have longer product lifecycles and less customer concentration than consumer casings. New customer projects enter mass production from June with a **double-digit revenue contribution** expected.
4. **Manufacturing margins are still decent.** Gross margin of **28.8%** on the remaining business.

The counter-arguments:

- **The operating business is collapsing, not declining.** Monthly revenue down **21%, 25%, 36%, 48%, 55%**. New projects must scale faster than the legacy business disappears, and they are starting from a small base.
- **The profit is not operating profit.** A **6.45% operating margin** is what the company actually earns from making things. Interest income depends on rates and on the asset base being maintained.
- **Earnings fell 42% because of currency and interest.** That is what a company reports when its results are financial rather than industrial — and it cuts both ways each year.
- **Cash flow is negative.** **−NT$262m of operating cash flow against NT$1.54bn of net profit** in 2026Q1.
- **A 4.11% return on equity** on a very large capital base. Being cheap relative to book is only valuable if the assets can be made to earn more, or returned.

A **discount-to-assets** thesis: buy a large balance sheet below its stated value, collect 5.57%, and judge management on whether the new operating business becomes real — while accepting that today's profit is financial, not industrial.

Catcher today runs **two businesses that look nothing alike**, and only one of them is on the income statement's top line:

- **Precision metalworking (the operating business).** CNC machining of aluminium, magnesium and other metals into casings, housings and structural components. This was built for **consumer electronics at extreme volume** — millions of identical parts for a product launch — and it is what has been contracting: monthly revenue down as much as **55% year-on-year**, with a **6.45% operating margin** in 2026Q1 on a **28.8% gross margin**, indicating that fixed costs now weigh heavily on a smaller base.
- **The financial asset base (where the profit is).** **NT$225.5bn of assets** against **NT$142.6bn of equity**, generating **interest income and investment returns** that produce a **40.69% net margin** from a 6.45% operating margin. The company's explanation of FY2025 — **FX turning negative, interest income lower, core operating profit stable** — describes this precisely.
- **What is being built.** **Medical devices** (long qualification, long lifecycles), **semiconductor equipment parts** (precision, high specification), **aerospace and drones**, and **AI servers**. All use the same machining competence; none has consumer electronics' volume volatility or single-customer concentration. **New customer projects entered mass production from June**, targeting a **double-digit revenue contribution**.
- **How capital is being returned.** A dividend of **NT$10.27** for FY2025 giving a **5.57% yield**, plus a **share buyback**. For a company trading at **0.73× book**, buying back stock is a rational use of capital — it retires equity below its stated value.

The levers are **new-programme ramp speed, the legacy decline rate, interest rates and investment returns, and capital return policy**. The strength is a balance sheet large enough to fund a multi-year transition and priced below its own book value. The vulnerability is that **a company whose profit is financial has to justify why it should remain a company** — the new operating business is the answer it is attempting, and it is starting from a base that is still shrinking faster than the new work is arriving.

The metal casing industry is a case study in what happens to a supplier when the customer's design changes.

- **How the business worked.** Machining a laptop or tablet casing from solid metal required thousands of CNC machines, tolerance control measured in microns, and the ability to ramp to enormous volume for a launch. That was a genuine barrier, and for a decade it made the handful of capable suppliers — Catcher among them — extremely profitable.
- **Why it stopped working.** Three forces at once: **product designs changed**, moving to different materials and constructions; **Chinese suppliers built comparable capability** with domestic cost and proximity advantages; and **customers consolidated supply**, which for a supplier means either winning more or losing everything. Catcher's revenue decline of **21% to 55% month by month** is the late stage of that process.
- **The pattern repeats across the collection.** **Pou Chen (9904)** in footwear and **Hon Hai (2317)** in assembly show the same structural exposure: extraordinary capability built for one customer's product, valuable exactly as long as that product is made that way.
- **What precision metalworking is still worth.** The competence does not disappear when the application does. **Medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace components and AI server hardware** all need precision machining, and all offer **longer product lifecycles and more diversified customers** than consumer electronics ever did. The trade is lower volume for higher margin and greater stability — and a slower ramp.
- **The financial-asset question.** Catcher is not alone among Taiwanese manufacturers in holding a financial base that produces more profit than operations — **Walsin Lihwa (1605)** elsewhere in this collection shows a similar pattern. In both cases the market applies a discount: **Catcher trades at 0.73× book, Walsin at 0.83×**. Investors consistently value a manufacturer's assets below stated worth when the manufacturing has stopped earning.

Catcher's position is **strong in capability and weak in application**. The industry truth is that **a contract manufacturer's moat is only as durable as its customer's design decisions** — and that rebuilding around new industries takes years during which the old revenue disappears faster than the new arrives.

**Strengths**
- **Large, lightly geared balance sheet**: **NT$225.5bn assets**, **NT$142.6bn equity**, **36.8% debt ratio** — trading at **0.73× book**.
- **Substantial non-operating income** from interest and investments, funding a **5.57% yield** and a **share buyback**.
- **Precision metalworking capability** transferable to medical, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and AI server hardware.
- Gross margin still **28.8%** on the remaining operating business.

**Weaknesses**
- **Revenue collapsing**: monthly declines of **21%, 25%, 36%, 48%, 55%**; Jan–May cumulative **−26.0%**.
- **Operating margin 6.45% against a 40.69% net margin** — profit is not operating profit.
- **2026Q1 operating cash flow −NT$262m** against **NT$1.54bn of net income**; **ROE 4.11%**.
- FY2025 earnings fell **42%** on currency and interest income alone.

**Opportunities**
- **New programmes in medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace/drones and AI servers** entering mass production from June, targeting a double-digit revenue contribution.
- **Buyback below book value** retiring equity at a discount.
- Rising rates supporting interest income.

**Threats**
- Legacy revenue disappearing faster than new programmes ramp.
- **Interest and FX reversals** — the same items that cut FY2025 earnings 42%.
- The market continuing to value the asset base below its stated worth.

- **The reported profit is not manufacturing profit (the central point).** **2026Q1: operating margin 6.45%, net margin 40.69%** — and the same gap in every recent quarter, reaching **18.5% against 81.1%** in 2024Q4. Any valuation or comparison based on net margin, net profit or price-to-earnings is measuring **interest, investment returns and currency**, not the business. The operating margin is the only figure that describes what Catcher does.
- **Revenue is falling at an accelerating rate.** **21%, 25%, 36%, 48%, 55%** year-on-year across recent months, with **May at NT$918m (−48.3%)**. New programmes in medical, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and AI servers began mass production only in June. They must scale against a base that is disappearing quickly.
- **The earnings driver is volatile in both directions.** FY2025's **42% decline** came from **FX turning negative and lower interest income**. Those items will move again, and neither is within management's control.
- **Cash flow diverges from profit.** **−NT$262m of operating cash flow against NT$1.54bn of net income** in 2026Q1 — the expected consequence of profit originating outside operations, and a reason not to read the net figure as cash earnings.
- **Low returns on a large capital base.** **4.11% return on equity** on **NT$142.6bn**. The discount to book (**0.73×**) is the market's judgment that the assets are not earning enough — a discount that only closes if returns rise or capital is returned.
- **A data defect was present in the source metrics.** The feed's **2024Q4 EPS row carried the FY2024 annual figure of NT$19.40**, not the quarter; it has been removed here. Anyone analysing this company from raw data should verify quarterly figures against the company's own reported annual results.

Catcher's outlook is a straightforward race: **can the new operating businesses become real before the old one finishes disappearing?** The axes to watch:

- **Revenue, and specifically its composition.** Monthly declines of up to **55%** describe the legacy business. **New customer projects in medical devices, semiconductor equipment, aerospace/drones and AI servers entered mass production from June**, with a **double-digit revenue contribution** targeted for the year. Whether the total revenue line stops falling is the single clearest signal.
- **Operating margin — not net margin.** **6.45% in 2026Q1.** This is what the company earns from manufacturing, and it is the only figure that will show whether the new programmes are profitable. Net margin will continue to be dominated by interest and investment returns and should be disregarded for operational assessment.
- **Operating cash flow.** **−NT$262m against NT$1.54bn of net profit.** Convergence would indicate the operating business is generating cash again.
- **Capital return.** A **5.57% yield** and a **buyback under way** at **0.73× book**. Continued repurchases below book value are accretive, and are a reasonable use of capital while returns on assets stay at **4.11%**.
- **Interest rates and currency.** The dominant swing factors in reported earnings, as FY2025's 42% decline demonstrated. Worth monitoring precisely because they are not a judgment on the business.

Bottom line: Catcher was one of the principal metal casing suppliers to the world's largest consumer electronics companies, and is now a company where **operating margin is 6.45% and net margin 40.69%** — the difference being **interest, investments and currency**, as management's own explanation of FY2025's fall from **NT$19.40 to NT$11.33** confirms. Revenue is down as much as **55% year-on-year**, operating cash flow is negative, and return on equity is **4.11%** — while the shares trade at **0.73× book** with a **5.57% yield** and a **buyback under way**, and new programmes in medical, semiconductor equipment, aerospace and AI server hardware begin ramping. Judge it on **operating margin and total revenue** — a balance sheet at a discount, attached to a manufacturing business being rebuilt from the ground up.
